document.title: Cable from Ambassador Dean to Secretary of State: "Subject: Discussion with Rajiv Gandhi on Afghanistan"
document.authors: Ambassador John Gunther Dean, U.S. Embassy New Delhi
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), A New Phase in the Great Game: U.S., Soviets, India, Pakistan vied to shape a new Afghanistan in late 1980s | National Security Archive
document.note: Dean summarizes Gandhi's July 10 account of his meeting with Gorbachev. Gandhi doubts Najibullah's national reconciliation, and found Gorbachev more concerned about fundamentalism than about Western-backed moderates, and not opposed to a role for the former King.

mentions.quote: IN THE COURSE OF MY PRIVATE MEETING WITH RAJIV GANDHI ON JULY 10 I GAVE HIM A PAPER
GANDHI SAID THAT HE PERSONALLY DOUBTED THAT THE PRESENT NATIONAL RECONCILIATION EFFORT BY THE NAJIBULLAH GOVERNMENT WOULD WORK
IN HIS CONVERSATIONS WITH GORBACHEV ON AFGHANISTAN, RAJIV FOUND THE SOVIET LEADER TO BE MORE CONCERNED ABOUT THE STRENGTHENING OF FUNDAMENTALISM
IN THE COURSE OF MY PRIVATE MEETING WITH RAJIV GANDHI ON JULY 10 I GAVE HIM A PAPER OUTLINING ALL THE POINTS
THIS GAVE ME AN OPPORTUNITY TO URGE HIM TO USE INDIA'S INFLUENCE WITH THE SOVIETS TO SEEK A SOVIET PULLOUT

events.description: Ambassador Dean met privately with Rajiv Gandhi, gave him a paper on US points about Afghanistan; Gandhi doubted Najibullah's reconciliation would work.
Cable reporting the Gandhi meeting sent to Washington.

Ambassador Dean met privately with Rajiv Gandhi, gave a paper of US points on Afghanistan; Gandhi doubted Najibullah's national reconciliation would work and saw no realistic coalition government acceptable to all sides.
Dean cabled State reporting his discussion with Gandhi on Afghanistan.
Gandhi's conversations with Gorbachev in Moscow on Afghanistan; Gorbachev more concerned about fundamentalism; former king's name raised with no opposition.

key_claims: Rajiv Gandhi personally doubted the Najibullah government's national reconciliation effort would succeed.
Gandhi thought Afghans were too divided for an easy political solution.
Gandhi found Gorbachev more concerned about strengthening fundamentalism than about moderate, Western-backed Afghan leaders.
Gandhi could not envision a coalition government acceptable to all sides.
The US urged India to use its influence with the Soviets to seek a pullout.
The US, UN and Pakistan were focusing on a neutral transitional regime, with a possible role for the former king, to which Moscow seemed not opposed.
